sentence: Ghosts every twentieth of a second, and the gaps keep growing: a falling ball speeds up the whole way down.
claim: Without air resistance, a falling object accelerates steadily at g ≈ 9.81 m/s², so it covers more distance in each equal interval.
source_title: OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, 3.5 Free Fall
note: Excerpt: free fall is motion with negligible air resistance and friction; g = 9.81 m/s² (9.78–9.83 by place). The ghost spacing grows by g·Δt² = 2.45 cm per 1/20 s step (computed).

sentence: It sails twenty centimeters across… and lands on the same frame.
claim: A level throw at 0.44 m/s from 1 m lands 19.9 cm out, after the same 0.4515 s as the drop, because horizontal and vertical motion are independent when air is negligible.
source_title: OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, 4.3 Projectile Motion
note: Excerpt (OER mirror of 4.3): 'Motions along perpendicular axes are independent and thus can be analyzed separately'; the section neglects air resistance. Computed: t = √(2 × 1 m / 9.81) = 0.4515 s; 0.44 × 0.4515 = 0.199 m. Cross-check fix: the change beat uses the 0.44 m/s throw.

sentence: Gravity pulls both balls down the same way.
claim: Without air resistance, heavy and light objects fall with the same acceleration.
source_title: OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, 3.5 Free Fall
note: Excerpt: without air resistance, heavier and lighter objects dropped from the same height reach the ground together (the section's hammer-and-feather example).

sentence: In sixteen thirty-eight, Galileo described a throw as two motions: a steady glide across, plus a fall.
claim: In Two New Sciences (1638), Fourth Day, Galileo treats a projectile's motion as compounded of a uniform horizontal motion and a naturally accelerated vertical one.
source_title: Galileo on Projectiles: Two New Sciences, Fourth Day (University of Virginia, Crew & de Salvio translation)
note: Excerpt: 'a body whose motion is compounded of two other motions, namely, one uniform and one naturally accelerated'. 1638 is the publication (Leiden); Museo Galileo dates the idea to about 1609, so the line says 'described', not 'showed'.

sentence: So at every tick, both sit at the same height.
claim: With air negligible, the vertical motion does not depend on the horizontal speed, so a thrown and a dropped ball released together stay level.
source_title: OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, 4.3 Projectile Motion
note: Same section as c2: perpendicular motions are independent; no horizontal acceleration when air resistance is negligible.

sentence: Throw twice as hard, then three times: forty centimeters out, then sixty.
claim: Level throws at 0.89 and 1.33 m/s from 1 m land 40.2 and 60.1 cm out, in the same 0.4515 s.
source_title: OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, 4.3 Projectile Motion
note: Computed: range = v × √(2h/g); 0.89 × 0.4515 = 0.402 m, 1.33 × 0.4515 = 0.601 m. Cross-check fix: replaces the 1×/2×/3× of 1.33 m/s (1.19 m and 1.78 m out), which broke the 60 cm rule and the drag badge.

sentence: Every row of ghosts stays level, and all four land on the same frame.
claim: Without air, all four balls fall in the same 0.4515 s; with air, the fastest (1.33 m/s) tennis ball would land 0.30 ms late, under the 1.67 ms of physics time in one frame at ×1/20.
source_title: OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, 4.3 Projectile Motion
note: Computed with the bible's drag.py model (tennis ball 57 g, 6.7 cm, Cd 0.55, air 1.2 kg/m³, 1 m drop): delays 0.04 / 0.15 / 0.30 ms at 0.44 / 0.89 / 1.33 m/s. A frame at 30 fps and ×1/20 is 1/600 s = 1.67 ms. The scene is drawn without air, and the takeaway's badge says so; 'always' is gone (at 3.99 m/s the delay is 1.66 ms, a full frame).

sentence: Measure it: nine gaps of a twentieth of a second.
claim: A 1 m fall takes 0.4515 s, so the strobe at 1/20 s fits nine whole gaps before the ball lands.
source_title: OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, 3.5 Free Fall
note: Computed: 0.4515 / 0.05 = 9.03; the ninth ghost (0.45 s) sits 6.7 mm above the floor and the knock comes 1.5 ms later. The drop is 1 m measured to the landing point (the rail is 100 cm up).

sentence: A one-meter fall takes about point four five seconds, thrown or dropped.
claim: From y = ½gt², a 1 m fall takes t = √(2 × 1 / 9.81) = 0.4515 s, whatever the sideways speed.
source_title: OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, 3.5 Free Fall
note: Computed. The section's g is 9.81 m/s²; 9.78–9.83 changes the time by under 0.2%.

sentence: Sideways speed changes where a ball lands, not when.
claim: With air negligible, horizontal speed sets the range but not the time of flight.
source_title: OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, 4.3 Projectile Motion
note: Shown with the badge 'air ignored: the fastest throw would land 0.3 ms late; a frame here is 1.7 ms' (c7's numbers).

sentence: For a level throw, only the height sets the clock.
claim: For a horizontal launch with air negligible, the time of flight is √(2h/g): it depends only on the height (and g).
source_title: OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, 4.3 Projectile Motion
note: 'Level throw' matters: a throw with an upward or downward component changes the time of flight. g is the same everywhere on the bench.

sentence: Next: why big swings and small swings take almost the same time.
claim: A pendulum's period is nearly independent of its amplitude, especially below about 15°; at 30° it is about 1.7% longer.
source_title: OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, 15.5 Pendulums (LibreTexts copy)
note: Excerpt: T = 2π√(L/g); 'the period is nearly independent of amplitude, especially if θ is less than about 15°'. The 1.7% at 30° is the cross-check's exact elliptic ratio (1.0174).
